subtype: Approach: seeking a second medical opinion [Action]
passage:
In the waiting room of the second specialist's clinic, Madhuri held a thick file on her knee. She had sorted every report by date: the scans, the blood tests, the first doctor's letter.
Her mother Rukmini kept twisting the corner of her shawl. "Will the first doctor be upset that we came?" Rukmini whispered.
"Doctors expect it, Amma," Madhuri said. "We want to understand, not to fight."
When their name was called, the specialist read every page without hurrying and asked two questions. Then the specialist explained the main plan matched what the first doctor had suggested, and described one extra option to ask about.
In the corridor Rukmini let out a long breath. "I feel I can begin now, knowing two of them see it the same way."

qa.q: How had Madhuri sorted the reports?
qa.a: Madhuri had sorted every report by date.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling in the waiting room?
qa.a: Rukmini was nervous and a little guilty, shown by twisting the shawl and asking if the first doctor would be upset.

qa.q: What could the family do about the extra option the specialist mentioned?
qa.a: They could take the extra option back to the first doctor and ask both specialists how it would fit the plan.

qa.q: How might the specialist see a family that brings the whole file?
qa.a: The specialist would find it easier to give a full opinion, since every report is in order and the questions can be answered.

grounding: The passage shows a family bringing all reports to a second qualified specialist before a long treatment, so decisions rest on two professional views.

subtype: Approach: seeking a second medical opinion [Action]
passage:
Dear Sonali,
Thank you for the long call last week. I wanted to write down what we decided, partly so I remember it.
The first hospital recommended a treatment for Appa that would last at least a year. Amma was ready to start immediately. I was scared to question it; it felt like doubting the doctor. But when you said, "For something this long, a second qualified opinion isn't disrespect," I realised I had wanted to ask all along.
So we asked the first doctor for copies of every report and scan, and she gave them without any fuss. On Monday we took the whole folder to a specialist at the medical college. She went through it for forty minutes. She agreed with the diagnosis and suggested one change in how the treatment would be timed.
Amma feels calmer now that two doctors see it the same way. We start next week.
Gopika

qa.q: Where did they take the folder of reports?
qa.a: To a specialist at the medical college.

qa.q: Why was Gopika scared to question the first recommendation?
qa.a: Gopika felt it would be like doubting the doctor and was afraid of seeming disrespectful.

qa.q: What made the second opinion useful?
qa.a: Bringing every report and scan let the second specialist review everything and confirm or adjust the plan.

qa.q: How does Amma feel after the second opinion?
qa.a: Amma feels calmer, since two doctors see it the same way.

grounding: It shows a family taking all reports to a second qualified specialist before a long treatment, so the decision rests on more than one professional view.

subtype: Approach: seeking a second medical opinion [Action]
passage:
Gurpreet, people ask if getting a second opinion was disloyal to our first doctor. It wasn't. I'm Jasleen, and when my mother's report came back last winter, the surgeon at the private hospital wanted to operate within the week. Mummy was terrified, Papa just wanted it over, and I felt everyone was waiting for me to say yes.
I asked for all the reports: the scans on a disc, the blood tests, the doctor's notes. The hospital gave them the same day. My cousin, who's a nurse, helped us get an appointment at the government medical college two days later.
That specialist spent an hour with the folder. She said surgery was right, but suggested one more test first to plan it better. The first surgeon agreed when we went back. Mummy went into the operation knowing two doctors had looked. That mattered to her more than anything.

qa.q: Where did they get the second opinion?
qa.a: At the government medical college, two days later.

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel when everyone seemed to be waiting for a yes?
qa.a: Jasleen felt pressured and anxious, carrying the decision for a terrified mother and a father who wanted it over.

qa.q: What steps made the second opinion possible so quickly?
qa.a: Asking for all the reports and scans, and a nurse cousin's help to book the medical college appointment.

qa.q: How did the second opinion matter to Mummy?
qa.a: Mummy felt reassured going into the operation, knowing two doctors had looked.

grounding: It shows a family taking all reports to a second qualified specialist before major treatment, so the decision is backed by two professional views.
